newsitem.title: INDIA: Strong rupee seen aiding Indian trade reforms.
newsitem.headline: Strong rupee seen aiding Indian trade reforms.

text.p: Surging foreign exchange reserves are pressuring the Indian rupee to rise, and have paved the way for an imminent round of import liberalisation, analysts said on Sunday.

They said the foreign exchange surge would cushion India in its efforts to end quantitative restrictions (QRs) on imports to which it is committed under World Trade Organisation (WTO) rules. Formal WTO consultations are due in June.
"I think this is the most opportune time," Rajesh Chadha, adviser at the National Council for Applied Economic Research (NCAER), told Reuters.
"We are still thinking of buying some more time (from WTO). But I say this is no longer required."
The government is scheduled around April 1 to announce a new trade policy which is expected to axe socialist controls as part of a reform programme launched in 1991.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) said on Saturday that India's foreign currency assets stood at $20.68 billion on March 14, compared with $16.8 billion a year ago.

More than $600 million of this came in just one week in an inflow of foreign investment in stocks and industry linked to India's February 28 budget for 1997-98 (April-March) that proposed to slash import duties and corporate taxation.
The rupee, currently at 35.8 rupees to the dollar, has been held steady by RBI intervention to prop up the dollar.
ICICI Securities and Finance Co (I-Sec) said last week the RBI had bought between $600 million and $800 million since the budget.
The foreign exchange inflow, which Finance Minister P. Chidambaram described as "an embarrassment of riches", could prove costly if it is allowed to linger, analysts said.
On the one hand, it would strengthen the rupee and hurt export competitiveness, on the other, it would add to the money supply in the banking system and stoke domestic inflation.
"RBI will not allow the rupee to harden. It has to be between 35 and 36 rupees to a dollar," said D.H. Pai Panandikar, corporate adviser to India's RPG industrial group.
"It cannot be allowed to harden because otherwise exports will suffer," he said.

Exports slowed to 6.2 percent in the April-January period of 1996-97, down from 22.12 percent in the same months of 1995-96. Inflation based on wholesale prices was at 7.78 percent, up from 5.13 percent a year ago.

Chadha said the rupee had already strengthened in recent months against the yen and the deutschemark and domestic inflation was further eroding its competitive advantage. "Obviously, exports have been hurt," he said.
Import liberalisation was needed because RBI intervention could stoke inflation. "We cannot afford to keep on adding rupees (into the system)," he said.
But Pai Panandikar said the RBI could control money supply by reducing its ample stock of government gilts.
"The threat of inflation is exaggerated," he said. "If the RBI plays its cards well, the additional money can be sponged out by sale of government securities. It would be very happy to sell."
Overall, the situation is seen as ripe for the Indian economy to emerge from an intricate web of trade controls that for decades included quotas, bans and high import tariffs.
"There is every likelihood that imports of consumer goods will be liberalised," Pai Panandikar said.

"We have to face the situation that we are among the last (few) countries with import controls in quantitative terms," he said. "We have to knock down restrictions. I think, in phases, government will remove these controls."
He said he expected the government to immediately ease imports in areas like textiles, in which India feels it has a competitive advantage.
